definition: Business intelligence (BI) consists of strategies, methodologies, and technologies used by enterprises for data analysis and management of business information to inform business strategies and business operations.
details: Common functions of BI technologies include reporting, online analytical processing, analytics, dashboard development, data mining, process mining, complex event processing, business performance management, benchmarking, text mining, predictive analytics, and prescriptive analytics. BI tools can handle large amounts of structured and sometimes unstructured data to help organizations identify, develop, and otherwise create new strategic business opportunities. They aim to allow for the easy interpretation of these big data. Identifying new opportunities and implementing an effective strategy based on insights is assumed to potentially provide businesses with a competitive market advantage and long-term stability, and help them make strategic decisions. Business intelligence can be used by enterprises to support a wide range of business decisions ranging from operational to strategic. Basic operating decisions include product positioning or pricing. Strategic business decisions involve priorities, goals, and directions at the broadest level. explainer.lead: Business intelligence (BI) turns an organization’s data into reports, analyses, and dashboards that people can use to make decisions. It matters because it connects everyday choices, such as pricing, with broader questions about goals and direction.

tiers.eli5: Business intelligence is like keeping a clear scorebook for a shop instead of guessing how it is doing. You gather information about sales and customers, organize it, and look for useful patterns. Those patterns can help the shop decide what to sell, how to price it, and what to improve.
tiers.practitioner: BI work commonly combines reporting, dashboards, online analytical processing, and data mining over large structured datasets, with some systems also handling unstructured data. Analysts may add text mining, predictive analytics, or prescriptive analytics depending on the decision. The main pitfalls are treating a dashboard as a decision by itself, overlooking the difference between operational and strategic questions, and assuming insights automatically create a competitive advantage.
tiers.paperLevel: BI = {strategies, methodologies, technologies} for analyzing data and managing business information to inform business strategy and operations. Its functions span descriptive reporting and analytical processing through predictive and prescriptive analytics, but its effectiveness depends on the available data and the interpretation and implementation of insights.

explainer.example: A retailer combines its sales data with information from its market and displays the results in a dashboard. The analysis shows weak sales for one product line, so managers use that evidence while reconsidering its positioning and price.

usedIn.name: Pricing decisions
usedIn.detail: Organizations analyze business information to support basic operating decisions about prices.

usedIn.name: Product positioning
usedIn.detail: BI helps teams evaluate where products fit and identify possible business opportunities.

usedIn.name: Strategic planning
usedIn.detail: Decision-makers use BI when setting broad priorities, goals, and directions.

usedIn.name: Business performance management
usedIn.detail: Reports and analytics help organizations monitor performance and compare results through benchmarking.

explainer.intuition: BI is the practice of turning scattered business information into a usable picture of what is happening and what might be worth doing next. Its value comes from informing human decisions, not merely from producing charts.
howItWorks: Gather structured and sometimes unstructured data relevant to the business.
Manage and analyze the data using BI methods and technologies.
Present findings through reports, dashboards, analytics, or mining results.
Use the findings to identify opportunities and support operational or strategic decisions.
explainer.whyItMatters: BI gives organizations a shared basis for choices ranging from daily operations to long-term direction. It can help reveal opportunities, although competitive advantage and stability depend on acting effectively on the insights.
misconceptions: BI is not just dashboard software; it also includes strategies and methodologies for managing and analyzing information.
A prediction or report does not automatically improve a business; decision-makers still have to interpret it and implement a strategy.

diagram.caption: BI connects business information to decisions through management, analysis, and accessible presentation.
